papers.notes: Paper IS SMOTE; there is no plain-SMOTE baseline. Proposed method as presented = SMOTE (k=5 nearest neighbours) combined with random majority under-sampling; ROC curves built by varying under-sampling at fixed SMOTE %. Comparisons: Under-C4.5 and Under-Ripper (plain under-sampling), Ripper Loss Ratio, Naive Bayes with varied priors (compared against SMOTE-C4.5), C4.5 decision thresholds (Phoneme), replication over-sampling (Mammography), SHRINK/one-sided selection (Oil, Tables 4-5, Acc+/Acc-). Only Table 3 gives per-dataset numbers (AUC, C4.5 only); Ripper and Naive Bayes results are ROC plots only (Figs 7-29) and AUCs for Ripper/Naive Bayes are explicitly not included. Table 5 (p.27, printed 347) gives Acc+/Acc- for 500% SMOTE + under-sampling 10%-800% on Oil vs Table 4 SHRINK 82.5%/60.9% and One-sided selection 76.0%/86.6%. Variants also introduced: SMOTE-NC (tested on Adult) and SMOTE-N (proposed, not tested). Paper notes exceptions: Pima (Naive Bayes dominates SMOTE-C4.5), Oil (Under-Ripper dominates SMOTE-Ripper), Can (overlap). A copy 'SMOTE (Original).pdf' exists in Binary folder; not read. Tables 3 (consistent cost matrices) and 4 (inconsistent) on p.4 report misclassification cost on all 20 data sets: BLIND as absolute cost, OLD and NEW as ratios to BLIND (lower is better); e.g. Table 3 imbalanced ave. OLD .930 ± .066, NEW .867 ± .087; Table 4 imbalanced ave. OLD .925 ± .101, NEW .893 ± .161. Table 5 (p.5) W/T/L (t-test 0.05): NEW vs OLD 13/7/0 on CCM, 13/6/1 on ICM; NEW vs BLIND 15/5/0 (CCM), 17/2/1 (ICM); OLD vs BLIND 8/12/0 (CCM), 7/13/0 (ICM). Cost matrices randomly generated in [1,10] (smallest-to-largest class misclassification cost biggest for imbalanced sets). SMOTE is not evaluated. Pages: PDF index 1-6 = printed 567-572.

papers.st: All seven main datasets (split into 48 two-class 'apportions') come from the UCR time series repository [17]. Seven further UCR datasets (CBF, Synthetic Control, OSU Leaf, Fish, Gun-Point, Trace, ECG) were used in an additional comparison whose results are only given online, not in the paper.
papers.cr: The datasets were chosen because they contain a large number of samples, to facilitate simulating scenarios of large class imbalance.
papers.pt: Started from seven 'balanced' UCR datasets. Multiclass sets (Adiac 37, FaceAll 14, 50words 50, SLeaf 15 classes) were made two-class by taking one class as positive and merging the rest as negative (one-vs-rest), giving several apportions per dataset (48 in total). The number of positive training samples was set to round numbers, no more than 50 percent of the available positives and no more than 50 per training set, to keep imbalance ratios high (7.6 to 60). Which classes were chosen as positive is not stated in the body text (Table 1 is an image).

papers.st: KEEL dataset repository (24 multi-class sets, mostly UCI originals), with KEEL partitions.
papers.cr: A data set is considered imbalanced when one class has less than 40% of the majority class, that is IR > 1.5. The authors justify the selection because the base classifier and plain OVO/OVA get low performance on many of these sets, and note IR alone is not the only difficulty. The study covers many classes and a wide IR range, but IR is the global max/min ratio with no per-class minority definition.

papers.q: We have selected a wide benchmark of 24 multiple-class data-sets from the KEEL data-set repository. we consider a data-set to be imbalanced when one of its classes has a distribution of examples below 40% of the number of instances that belong to the majority class; that is, if the IR is higher than 1.5.

papers.inh: Napierala, Stefanowski, Wilk (noisy and borderline examples)
papers.rec: new7 (PDF re-read 16 Oct, page refs in ai-draft/new7)
papers.st: 9 real-world datasets: 8 from the KEEL-dataset repository, plus acl, which the authors of ref. [45] (Slowinski et al.) supplied. 30 synthetic 2-D datasets (sub-cluster, clover, paw shapes; IR 5 or 7; 5 disturbance ratios) come from the family in ref. [40]/[46] and are on the paper's web page. 36 noisy versions were built by adding class or attribute noise (20%, 40%) to the 9 real-world datasets.
papers.cr: Real-world datasets: 'The choice of the real-world datasets was based on the work on imbalanced classification with noisy and borderline examples presented in [40]'; also 'As the number of noisy examples is quite high compared to the size of the minority class these data sets are chosen to study their impact.' Synthetic: 'This paper uses the family of synthetic datasets used in prior research on the role of borderline examples [40].'
papers.pt: Multi-class real-world datasets became binary by taking the union of one or more classes as positive and the rest as negative. Table 1 names each minority class (e.g. ecoli imU, newthyroid hyper, cleveland positive). Synthetic data were generated with 600 examples at IR=5 or 800 examples at IR=7, a minority class split into sub-regions (5 parts, or 3 for paw) inside a uniform majority, and borderline disturbance ratios DR = 0/30/50/60/70%. Noisy versions: class noise uses a pairwise scheme where a majority example is relabelled minority with probability x/100. Attribute noise: each attribute is corrupted separately in about x% of examples with a uniform random value (numeric) or a random domain value (nominal), x = 20% or 40%.
papers.q: [p.190 (printed)] This work focuses on binary classification problems (the minority versus the majority class) with examples randomly and uniformly distributed in the two-dimensional real-value space.; [p.191 (printed)] In such a way, 30 synthetic datasets with the above mentioned properties have been managed, all of which are available on the web-page associated with this paper.; [p.191 (printed)] In such a way, two different noise levels will be introduced into them: x = 20% and x = 40%. papers.notes: Binary-only paper (KEEL highly imbalanced, IR 8.10-41.40). Metric is AUC only (G-mean and F-measure explicitly not used, p.6). Per-dataset AUC for SplitBal+MaxDistance across six classifiers exists in Table 8 p.9 (Naive Bayes SplitBal Avg 0.8811). SMOTE appears only as average AUC (Table 9), ranks (Table 10) and Nemenyi plots (Fig. 2). Other variants: five ensemble rules (MaxDistance, MinDistance, ProDistance, MajDistance, SumDistance) vs Kittler rules (Tables 4-7). Weka default params, IBK K=5; SMOTE parameters not stated in paper. Fuzzy comparison Chi3-GTS/Chi5-GTS in Table 11 p.11.

papers.st: Chapter states only publicly available datasets. Vehicle, Ecoli, Pima, Balance, Liver, Wine, Breast Tissue, Libra, LEV, Iris, Heart, Glass, Haberman, Eucalyptus, Heating, Segment. Standard UCI-style benchmarks, but the repository is not named and LEV/Eucalyptus/Heating may come from elsewhere.
papers.cr: Not stated; appears to follow prior oversampling work. The selection overlaps heavily with the MWMOTE benchmark (Glass, Libra, Vehicle, Breast Tissue, Pima, Yeast) and with ADASYN/RAMOBoost (Vehicle van-vs-rest, Pima, Segment). Datasets cover moderate imbalance and varied size and dimension.
papers.pt: Multiclass to two-class conversion. 4-fold stratified CV repeated 3 times. RBF-SVM, logistic regression, kNN, LDA tuned by stratified CV on G-mean. Friedman plus Holm tests.
papers.q: The proposed A-SUWO method was evaluated on 16 publicly available datasets and compared with eight other oversampling techniques

papers.st: UCI Machine Learning Repository. Table 1 gives sample count, feature count, imbalance ratio and release year per dataset.
papers.cr: Datasets were randomly chosen from UCI for empirical testing, with most released within the past 10 years (release years 1988 to 2014). Multiclass datasets are converted to binary by keeping the smallest class as minority and merging the rest. They span financial to medical applications, which motivates the use of several metrics.
papers.pt: Multiclass to binary: keep the smallest class, merge the rest. 10 rounds of 10-fold CV. Six classifiers with hyper-parameters tuned by CV. Precision, recall, F1, G-score, AUC; Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
papers.q: 30 real-world datasets were randomly chosen from the UCI machine learning repository for empirical testing of CGMOS. Most of the datasets were released within the past 10 years.

papers.cr: Data sets have at least one class with significantly smaller number of instances than other classes. Table 1 lists, per data set, which classes are treated as minority and majority, so minority/majority structure is explicit and multi-minority is common (Yeast has nine minority classes against CYT). Sizes, numbers of classes (3 to 26) and IR (1.09 to 439.6) were varied.

papers.irdef: "Imbalance ratio or IR is computed as the proportion of the number of majority class examples to the number of minority class examples [40]. The class with maximum number of instances is the majority class and the class with minimum number of examples is the minority class."
papers.notes: No per-dataset numbers anywhere in the paper; results only as Friedman mean ranks (Tables 2,4,6) and Bonferroni-Dunn rank differences (Tables 3,5,7) for MAUC, G-mean, precision, recall, F-measure with C4.5, KNN (K=5), Ripper (Weka). Other mean ranks MDO vs SMOTE: C4.5 MAUC 1.1750 vs 2.2250, F-measure 1.9000 vs 2.7250; KNN MAUC 1.2000 vs 2.6500, G-mean 2.1000 vs 2.4750; Ripper MAUC 1.2000 vs 2.5500, G-mean 2.1000 vs 2.7750. SMOTE applied to each minority class separately (one-vs-majority style); ADASYN and Borderline-SMOTE used with OAA (p.3). Precision/recall/F-measure computed for the minority class only. Parameters: K=5 all methods, ADASYN beta=1, MDO K1=5, K2=10. Table 1 text verified against rendered page 9 image. No supplementary file referenced.

papers.st: Most from UCI. Eight (housing5, housing10, SWD, LEV, machine, ESL, ERA, ERA5) are ordinal regression benchmark sets. Table 1 shows which original classes form each experimental class.
papers.cr: Stated: these experimental data sets vary in size, class distribution, feature number and IR to ensure a reliable assessment of performance. The authors note there is no criterion to separate minority and majority classes in multiclass imbalance, so they call classes with more or fewer than M/L instances (the mean class size) majority or minority. Several sets were constructed by merging or sub-selecting classes to create multiclass imbalance.
papers.pt: Average of 10 runs of stratified 10-fold CV. C4.5, AdaBoost.M1, MLP; metrics MG, MAUC and per-class recall/precision/F.
papers.q: 27 multiclass imbalanced data sets are used in our experiments. As there is no criterion to distinguish minority classes and majority classes in multiclass imbalance data, we simply classify the classes whose instances size greater (/smaller) than M/L as the majority (/minority) classes.

papers.irdef: Overall imbalance degree for multiclass data: IR = sum_{i=1}^{C-1} sum_{j>i} (N_i/N_j - 1), Eq. (3), classes sorted in descending size; IR = 0 if all classes equal size. Minority/majority classes: classes with size smaller/greater than M/L.
papers.notes: Per-dataset results only in Supplementary (Tables S3-S20); main paper gives averages/ranks (Tables 2, 4) and Wilcoxon tests (Tables 3, 5, 6). Metric priority G-mean: MG used. Other per-dataset tables: MAUC (S5,S6), recall/precision of smallest class (S7-S10), F-measure SL-SMOTE vs SMOM only (S11), Experiment 2 with SMOTE (k=12) (S13-S16; S13 = MG). Classifiers: C4.5, AdaBoost.M1(C4.5), MLP, NB (Weka). SMOM params k1=12, k2=8, rTh=5/8, nTh=10, w1=0.2, w2=1/2, r1=1/3, r2=0.2. Main text extraction garbled SWD/LEV/ERA/ERA5 M as '10 0 0'; values read from rendered page 8 image (1000). Table S3 text extraction was clean; bold marks verified from rendered image. 'voice9_6' etc. printed with underscore in Table 1 (rendered as 'voice9 6' in S3 text layer).

papers.st: 15 benchmarks from UCI and KEEL. Pre2D and PreND are real data from the China Meteorological Administration (888 automatic weather stations, North China, 2004-2015; rain/snow/sleet) with a time-based train/test split.
papers.cr: Only data sets with IR > 1.5 were kept, and sets whose smallest class had fewer than 10 samples were excluded so that cross-validation is fair. The set deliberately mixes numeric and mixed-type data because AMDO generalises MDO to mixed attributes. Classes with under 10 samples in Ecoli and Nursery were removed and missing-value samples dropped.
papers.pt: Removed samples with missing values (Dermatology); removed classes with fewer than 10 samples (Ecoli, Nursery). 5-fold CV x 10 runs, except Pre2D/PreND which use a fixed time split.
papers.q: only data sets with IR>1.5 are selected. we do not include data sets where the number of samples in the minimum class is less than 10.

papers.st: 36 frequently used datasets in class-imbalance classification from the UCI and KEEL repositories.
papers.cr: The 36 datasets were chosen because they are frequently used in class-imbalance classification. They deliberately vary in size, imbalance ratio and number of features to test robustness under different situations. Many are nearly linearly separable and others heavily overlapped, which suits the overlap-based method.
papers.pt: 80:20 train/test split with 10-fold CV; Random Forest (500 trees) as classifier; binary datasets only.
papers.q: In all experiments, 36 frequently used datasets in class-imbalance classification were selected. These datasets are obtained from UCI and KEEL repositories, vary in terms of size (129 to 5472 instances), imbalance ratio (1.87 to 129.44), and number of features (3 to 19).

papers.st: MNIST (LeNet-5), CIFAR-10 (All-CNN), ILSVRC-2012 subset of ImageNet (ResNet-10, 1000 classes).
papers.cr: Three benchmarks of increasing complexity, all perfectly balanced in their original form, so imbalance can be induced in a fully controlled way and conclusions from a simple task can be checked on harder ones. Two imbalance profiles are defined: step imbalance (mu = fraction of minority classes, rho = majority/minority ratio) and linear imbalance. Minority classes are randomly chosen (MNIST, 50 repeats) or fixed as the lowest labels (CIFAR-10).
papers.pt: CIFAR-10: global contrast normalisation plus ZCA whitening, no augmentation. ImageNet: resize shorter side to 256, random 224x224 crop and mirroring, majority classes reduced from 1200 to 1000. All nets trained from scratch; multi-class ROC AUC.
papers.q: The first type is step imbalance. In step imbalance, the number of examples is equal within minority classes and equal within majority classes but differs between the majority and minority classes.
rows: other: MNIST benchmark (LeCun, Bottou, Bengio, & Haffner, 1998)

papers.irdef: ρ = max_i{|C_i|} / min_i{|C_i|} (ratio between number of examples in majority and minority classes, Eq. 2); step imbalance also uses µ = fraction of minority classes (Eq. 1); linear imbalance uses same ρ with linear interpolation of class sizes
papers.notes: Comparative study, not a new method: proposed = random minority oversampling ('Oversampling'). SMOTE not evaluated. All three datasets are 10- or 1000-class multiclass with artificially induced step/linear imbalance on the training set; test sets kept balanced. MNIST and CIFAR-10 results (Figs. 3-7) are plots only. Table 4 Undersampling values: 96.85, 94.98, 88.35, 84.08, 83.74. Supplementary Appendix A (CIFAR-10 reshuffled splits) contains plots only; Appendix B (convergence plots) and Appendix C (confusion matrices) not used for numeric comparison. Main comparator: Baseline (do-nothing).

papers.st: 12 UCI datasets; 19 KEEL imbalanced datasets; 10 simulated variations of MADELON generated with scikit-learn. Undersampled UCI variants add higher IR.
papers.cr: Not explicitly justified beyond using widely used public UCI and KEEL imbalanced benchmarks. Multiclass sets were binarised one-vs-rest (smallest class as minority) and undersampled to create higher-IR versions so the method is tested across a wide range of imbalance severity. Simulated MADELON data added as a difficult binary problem with high dimensionality and very low minority counts.
papers.pt: Multiclass binarised one-vs-rest; random undersampling of minority to raise IR; stratified 5-fold CV repeated 5 times; oversamplers balance to 1:1; grid search per metric.
papers.q: To evaluate k-means SMOTE, 12 imbalanced datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository are used. each of the aforementioned datasets was randomly undersampled to generate up to six additional datasets. Furthermore, 19 imbalanced datasets were selected from the KEEL repository.

Classifiers LR, KNN (k 3,5,8), GBM (50,100,200 trees); abstract highlights none, LR listed first, but only KNN has per-dataset plot. papers.st: All from the KEEL imbalanced-data repository. Noise-corrupted versions are synthetic: label noise following Zhu et al. (majority-to-minority flips at 0 to 20%) and feature noise following Saez et al. (Gaussian noise per feature).
papers.cr: Datasets were chosen to vary in size, number of features and degree of imbalance, which the authors say ensures a reliable assessment. All are public KEEL sets, so they are reproducible. papers.q: Overall, 34 two-class datasets with a varying level of imbalance were used throughout the experiments. Out of them, 10 were randomly chosen for the preliminary analysis, while the remaining 24 were used for the remainder of the experiments.

papers.st: Synthetic checkerboard (16 Gaussian components, 1000 positives vs 10000 negatives); Credit Fraud (European card-holders 2013); Payment Simulation; Record Linkage (German cancer registry record pairs); KDDCUP-99 (DOS vs PRB and DOS vs R2L).
papers.cr: Real tasks are large-scale, extremely imbalanced datasets from practical applications (fraud, record linkage, intrusion detection), chosen to test efficiency and robustness on massive noisy data. KDDCUP-99 multi-class data were converted into two binary problems by pairing majority DOS with minority PRB or R2L. The synthetic checkerboard controls class overlap while keeping size and IR fixed.

papers.q: we present the results of our experimental study on one synthetic and five real-world extremely imbalanced datasets.

papers.st: 40 KEEL datasets; 10 large UCI datasets with over 4000 instances, two with over 160 features; 2 real datasets collected by the authors: Internet video traffic (Wireshark captures from 5 video sites, 256-dim BCD features) and esophageal cancer clinical text records (2861 records, 750-dim vectors after NLP).

The UCI sets were chosen for being large (>4000 instances) and in two cases high-dimensional (>160 features) to test scalability and robustness beyond the small KEEL sets. The two real datasets show applicability to real imbalanced problems in network traffic and medical text.
papers.pt: 10-fold CV. Multi-class sets converted to binary with the smallest class as minority. Video-traffic features from BCD filtered with Weka CfsSubsetEval; esophageal text converted to 750-dim vectors by NLP.
papers.q: 40 public data sets from the KEEL data repository, and 10 large data sets from the UCI machine learning repository are used. Two real application data sets collected by ourselves are also used for the experiments.

papers.st: Own experiments: Yeast4, Yeast5, Yeast6 from UCI, each 10 attributes and about 1484 samples (51/44/35 minority).
papers.cr: The 3 datasets were chosen because they are routinely used by many oversampling methods, they are binary, and they stay imbalanced after some majority samples are hidden. The review's central argument is that oversampling is judged only by downstream classification metrics on a few benchmark datasets, with no check that synthesised samples are realistic.
papers.pt: Hide 10/25/50% of the majority class at random, oversample, then compare synthetic points to the hidden majority points with Hassanat distance; 5 repeats averaged.
papers.q: We employ three real-life datasets to put our validation system to the test, namely Yeast4, Yeast5, and Yeast6, which are routinely used by many oversampling methods.

papers.cr: Standard UCI/KEEL multi-class benchmarks with 3 to 11 classes. Instances with missing values were removed, classes with fewer than 10 instances dropped, and class sizes adjusted in some datasets to obtain the required imbalance. Minority classes are not predefined: GLOS identifies them by comparing a class-level discreteness value with instance-level dispersion. The paper explicitly studies multi-minority, multi-majority and mixed cases by re-cutting Segment and Texture.
papers.pt: Removed missing-value instances; removed classes with fewer than 10 instances; adjusted class sizes in some datasets. C4.5 with OAA/OAO/OAHO/A&O decomposition. 5-fold CV x 10 runs.
papers.q: 21 multi-class data sets from the UCI repository and KEEL repository are selected. we removed the instances with missing values, removed the classes with less than 10 instances in each data set and adjusted the size of classes in some data sets.

papers.cr: Datasets were chosen to be diverse: multi-majority, multi-minority and gradual class-size configurations, different class overlap levels and different numbers of classes. papers.cr: Datasets, baselines, classifiers, metrics and tests were fixed in a preregistered protocol before running evaluation to avoid selective reporting. KEEL provides the standard imbalanced benchmark; 8 larger UCI datasets test generalisation beyond the KEEL regime and scalability. A disjoint tuning suite prevents leakage.
papers.pt: Per-fold standardisation fitted on the training fold; nominal attributes one-hot encoded; missing numeric values imputed with training-fold mean; multiclass binarised smallest-class-versus-rest; 4 classifiers; 11460 fold-level evaluations.
papers.q: The primary evaluation suite comprises 37 binary imbalanced datasets from the KEEL repository, with imbalance ratios from 1.8 to 41.4 and dimensions from 3 to 34. A scale suite of 8 larger datasets from the UCI repository, with sample sizes up to 20,000 and dimensions up to 166.

papers.cr: Adopted wholesale from the VS-SMOTE benchmark to allow direct comparison using the same dataset identifiers and published baseline results. The suite spans mild to severe imbalance so oversampling behaviour can be analysed by imbalance regime (IR<5, 5-15, >=15).
papers.pt: Repeated stratified CV; oversampling only on the training fold; CatBoost classifier; baseline results copied from the VS-SMOTE paper.
papers.q: We evaluate QC-SMOTE on the 30 real-world binary imbalanced datasets used in the VS-SMOTE benchmark, with imbalance ratios ranging from IR = 1.82 to IR = 32.73.

A-SUWO.title: Oversampling Methods for Imbalanced Dataset Classification and their Application to Gynecological Disorder Diagnosis (Ch. 3: Adaptive Semi-Unsupervised Weighted Oversampling (A-SUWO) for Imbalanced Datasets)
A-SUWO.ctab: Table 3.1, printed p.35 (PDF index not determined)

AB-SMOTE.title: AB-SMOTE: An Affinitive Borderline SMOTE Approach for Imbalanced Data Binary Classification
AB-SMOTE.irdef: not stated in paper as a formula; Table I column 'IR Ratio' printed as percentages. Selection wording: 'if minority number of instances are less than 40% of the number of instances of the majority class, the dataset is considered unbalanced'

ADASYN.title: ADASYN: Adaptive Synthetic Sampling Approach for Imbalanced Learning
ADASYN.irdef: degree of class imbalance d = ms/ml (Eq. 1), where ms = # minority, ml = # majority, d in (0,1]

AMDO.title: AMDO: an Over-Sampling Technique for Multi-Class Imbalanced Problems
AMDO.irdef: IR is computed as the proportion of nmaj to nmin, where nmin is the smallest number of class samples among the minority classes. A data set is considered to be imbalanced if IR>1.5

Borderline-SMOTE.title: Borderline-SMOTE: A New Over-Sampling Method in Imbalanced Data Sets Learning
Borderline-SMOTE.irdef: not stated in paper (only 'Percentage of minority class' is reported in Table 2)

CBHSID.title: A Hybrid Sampling Approach for Imbalanced Binary and Multi-Class Data Using Clustering Analysis
CBHSID.irdef: number of data samples in the majority class over the number of data samples in the minority class, for both binary and multi-class datasets

CISO.title: Certified Interpolation Oversampling: Per-Instance Safety Guarantees for Imbalanced Learning
CISO.ctab: Table 1, p.16 (KEEL 37 + UCI 8); Table 2, p.18 (5 tuning)

COG-OS.title: Local Decomposition for Rare Class Analysis
COG-OS.irdef: not stated in paper (imbalance described by CV, Coefficient of Variation of class sizes; no IR used)
COG-OS.ctab: Table 2, p.5 (printed 818); also Table 8, p.7 (printed 820) for kddcup99data and modified binary sets; Table 3, p.6 (printed 819) for sampled imbalanced binary sets

CTGAN / TVAE.title: Modeling Tabular Data using Conditional GAN

Cluster-SMOTE.title: Combating Imbalance in Network Intrusion Datasets

ClusterCentroids.title: Cluster-based under-sampling approaches for imbalanced data distributions

DGOT.title: Diffusion GAN-Based Oversampling for Imbalanced Tabular Data
DGOT.irdef: IR = N_maj / N_min (Eq. 26); for multi-class datasets, IR is the ratio between the number of instances in the class with the most and those with the fewest instances.

DLexiBoost.title: Boosting with Lexicographic Programming: Addressing Class Imbalance without Cost Tuning
DLexiBoost.irdef: measured as the ratio of the number of representatives from the largest and the smallest classes
DLexiBoost.ctab: none (per-dataset IR and |C| only in Supplement Tables 1,3,5,6; n_instances/n_features not printed for KEEL sets)

DSRBF / Static-SMOTE.title: A dynamic over-sampling procedure based on sensitivity for multi-class problems
DSRBF / Static-SMOTE.irdef: not stated in paper (no IR defined; paper reports p* = minimum of the estimated prior probabilities, p* = min{f_i/N}, used in Eq. (8) and Table 3)

EMDO.title: Evolutionary Mahalanobis Distance-Based Oversampling for Multi-Class Imbalanced Data Classification
EMDO.irdef: IRmax = Nmax/Nmin, Nmin = min_j(N_j), Nmax = max_j(N_j) (Eq. 47)

EasyEnsemble / BalanceCascade.title: Exploratory Undersampling for Class-Imbalance Learning
EasyEnsemble / BalanceCascade.irdef: Ratio IS THE SIZE OF MAJORITY CLASS DIVIDED BY THAT OF MINORITY CLASS (Table II caption); also 'level of imbalance (ratio of size of the majority class to minority class)' (p.1)

FW-SMOTE.title: FW-SMOTE: A feature-weighted oversampling approach for imbalanced classification
FW-SMOTE.irdef: not stated in paper (Table 1 column 'IR' = Imbalance Ratio; no formula given)

G-SMOTE.title: Geometric SMOTE a geometrically enhanced drop-in replacement for SMOTE
G-SMOTE.irdef: "the ratio between the majority class and each of the minority classes"; Table 1 IR = Majority instances / Minority instances

GAMO.title: Generative Adversarial Minority Oversampling
GAMO.irdef: Imbalance Ratio (IR: ratio of the number of representatives from the largest class to that of the smallest class)
GAMO.ctab: none (no characteristics table in main paper; counts given in Sec 4.1-4.4 text; non-image properties in Supplement Table 7, p.8)

GDHS.title: GDHS: An efficient hybrid sampling method for multi-class imbalanced data classification
GDHS.irdef: IR = sum_{i=1}^{M-1} sum_{j>i} (|C_i|/|C_j| - 1), classes sorted in descending size (Eq. 17; formula garbled in text extraction, reconstructed from fragments)

GDO.title: Gaussian Distribution Based Oversampling for Imbalanced Data Classification
GDO.irdef: IR = n_maj / n_min (Eq. 25): ratio between the number of majority and minority class instances
GDO.ctab: Table 2, p.7 (KEEL, IR only) and Table 3, p.8 (large); Table 4, p.8 (video traffic)

GLOS.title: Global-local information based oversampling for multi-class imbalanced data

GMMSampling.title: GMMSampling: a new model-based, data difficulty-driven resampling method for multi-class imbalanced data
GMMSampling.irdef: a ratio of the biggest class size to the cardinality of the smallest class

GOIO.title: GOIO: Generative Oversampling Approach to Class Imbalance and Overlap of Tabular Data
GOIO.ctab: Table I, p.7 (real-world, image); Table II, p.7 (artificial, image)

HDE.title: A hybrid data-level ensemble to enable learning from highly imbalanced dataset
HDE.irdef: IR = ratio of majority instances to minority instances (Introduction)

INOS.title: Integrated Oversampling for Imbalanced Time Series Classification
INOS.irdef: IM-ratio: 'the number of negative samples divided by the number of positive samples' (computed on training set per Table 1)

KNNOR.title: KNNOR: An oversampling technique for imbalanced datasets
KNNOR.irdef: IR = N- / N+ (N- = number of majority (negative) samples, N+ = number of minority (positive) samples) (Eq. 11; extracted text renders it as 'IR = N−N+')

overview._about: เนื้อหาแท็บ 'ร่าง manuscript' ในหน้า Atlas สรุปว่า Data section มีอะไร ผู้อ่านได้อะไร และสังเคราะห์อะไรได้ ตัวเลขทุกตัวมาจาก out/verified_*.csv และ out/data_handling_summary.json (ตรวจกับ PDF 18 ต.ค. 2026) ตัวเลขชื่อ dataset และผลเทียบกระทบยอดแล้วด้วย build/reconcile_counts.py (19 ต.ค. 2026) แก้ไฟล์นี้แล้วรัน python3 build/make_atlas.py
overview.question: การที่งานวิจัยตระกูล SMOTE เลือกและจัดการข้อมูลแบบที่ทำกันอยู่ ส่งผลต่อความน่าเชื่อถือของผลที่รายงานอย่างไร และงานถัดไปควรรายงานข้อมูลอย่างไร
overview.scope: corpus 76 paper (ตรงกับ Section 7 ของ P) ใช้ 73 paper ที่มีการประเมินผลบนข้อมูล · dataset 1,654 รายการ · ผลเทียบกับ SMOTE 835 แถว จาก 44 paper (รายชุด 834 แถว + ค่าเฉลี่ยของ KNNOR 1 แถว) · ทุกค่ามีเลขตารางและหน้า และตรวจกับ PDF แล้ว
overview.gap: survey ที่มีอยู่ยังไม่มีเล่มไหนวิเคราะห์ด้านข้อมูลอย่างเป็นระบบ Fernández et al. (2018, JAIR) ไม่มี protocol การค้น, Pradipta (2021) ไม่มีส่วนข้อมูล, Hassanat (2022) วิเคราะห์ตัววิธี ไม่ใช่ข้อมูล

manuscript.html:
How the SMOTE Literature Uses Data

A reader who wants to compare two SMOTE variants, or to choose a benchmark for a new one, needs answers to questions that the papers rarely answer together. Can the numbers that two papers report on a dataset of the same name be compared? How broad is the evidence behind the benchmarks the field relies on? When a paper reports that its method beats SMOTE, on what kind of data does that happen, and can a reader check it? This section answers these questions from the 1,654 dataset entries and 835 comparisons with SMOTE (834 per dataset and one average over datasets) that we extracted from the 76 papers of our corpus. Three of them (ENN, AdaBoost and one review) contain no evaluation on data, so counts below use the 73 papers with an evaluation on data; Tomek links is kept because it illustrates its method on one synthetic two-class set.

The central observation is that the evidence for a new oversampler is only as interpretable as the description of its data, and in this literature that description is often incomplete: the same name can denote different tasks, modifications are frequently undeclared, and a sizeable share of papers report results that cannot be traced back to individual datasets.

Extraction Procedure

For every paper we read the full text and any supplementary file in our collection, and recorded each dataset as printed, including spelling, with its group in the paper, source repository, size, number of features and classes, minority and majority counts, and the imbalance ratio where the paper prints them, together with the table and page they come from. For each dataset we also recorded how it reached the experiment: original (used as distributed, with its native classes), repository-defined (a two-class split published by a repository such as KEEL or imbalanced-learn, used as is), modified (the authors chose the minority classes, merged or dropped classes, set a threshold, undersampled or injected noise), or synthetic (generated by the authors). Where a paper did not state its source, two fixed rules were applied and flagged: names that follow the KEEL file convention (for example ecoli-0-1_vs_5, yeast4) were labelled repository-defined, and common names in multiclass papers with no stated change were labelled original. Two further rules were fixed before counting: a set that is two-class in its source and is used without comment was labelled original, and a set from which the authors removed rows (for example, records with missing values) or attributes was labelled modified.

For the results we copied, per dataset, the printed score of the proposed method and of SMOTE from one results table selected by a fixed rule: G-mean, else AUC, else F-measure, else accuracy; the classifier highlighted in the abstract, else the first reported; the unperturbed condition. We recorded values rather than wins so that any definition of a win can be applied later. Plain SMOTE was distinguished from SMOTE embedded in a multiclass or ensemble wrapper (Static-SMOTE, OVO-SMOTE [fernandez2013analysing], SMOTE-all, SMOTE+AdaBoost). Values printed in a paper are never overwritten; corrections against the source repository are stored beside them with their justification. Every extracted value was then checked against the PDF a second time: a value was accepted when the dataset name and its numbers appear on the same line of the cited page, and every table that is printed as an image or whose text layer is garbled was read from the rendered page instead. All 1,654 dataset entries and 835 comparisons passed this check.

Evidence: ai-draft/full/SCHEMA.md; build/full_extraction.py; KEEL and multiclass rules approved by Toon 18 Oct, rules A and B 18 Oct; 454 extraction notes in out/full_uncertain.csv, each resolved in out/uncertain_resolution.csv; second check: build/verify_pdf.py, out/visual_checks.json, out/verified_.csv.
[ช่องของ Toon] Add the blind re-extraction agreement rate once phase 5 is done.

The Benchmark Landscape

The 73 papers with an evaluation on data list 1,654 dataset entries. One of them, the single toy example in Tomek links, is a description rather than a name and is set aside here, leaving 1,653 named entries. These reduce to 771 distinct names once names are lower-cased, text in parentheses is dropped, and underscores and spaces are treated alike; hyphens and dots are kept, so page-blocks and pageblocks remain two names. Most names appear once: 546 of the 771 occur in a single paper. Counted by exact name, ecoli appears in 26 papers, yeast in 22 and glass in 19; counted together with the splits derived from them (for example yeast4 or glass-0-1-6_vs_2), the yeast and ecoli families each appear in 39 papers and the glass family in 36, about half of the 73.

A count of datasets therefore overstates the diversity of the evidence. Many distinct names are splits of the same few sources, so a paper that reports forty datasets may be testing on a handful of underlying distributions.

What the reader should do.

Report the source family of each dataset alongside the count, so that readers can see how many independent sources stand behind a claim.

Evidence: out/verified_datasets.csv; counts reproduced by build/reconcile_counts.py (out/reconcile_counts.json): rule R1 sets aside the Tomek links placeholder (row 1558, kept in the file), R2 normalises with build/analyse_dataset_usage.py norm(), R3 gives exact-name and prefix (family) counts. With the placeholder the counts are 772 and 547; removing all punctuation would leave 678 names. The 605 names of the 6 Oct list are superseded by the 771 of the full re-read.

How Datasets Are Chosen and Modified

Table 1
How the Papers Choose and Obtain Their Data. Top: paper level, 73 papers with an evaluation on data. Bottom: dataset entries.
Reason given for the choice of datasets (papers)
Own reason (diversity, difficulty, application, …) 48
Cites prior work 14
“Widely used” only 3
Not stated 8
Benchmark list adopted from earlier work, declared (papers) 20 (wholesale 11)
Binarised, minority rule not stated (papers) 8 of 37
How each dataset entry reached the experiment
Original 534
Repository-defined (KEEL, imbalanced-learn) 470
Modified by the authors 331
Synthetic 120
Cannot be told from the paper 199

Table 1 shows that modification by the authors is common: 331 of 1,654 dataset entries were changed by the authors themselves, and for 199 the paper does not let a reader tell how the data were obtained. Eleven papers give no reason for their choice of datasets or only call them widely used.

Modification is not a fault in itself: binarising a multiclass set or raising the imbalance ratio are legitimate ways to probe a method. What matters for the reader is whether the modification is declared where a reader looks for it. A KEEL file name such as yeast-0-5-6-7-9_vs_4 declares its split; a paper that prints only “Yeast” after choosing its own minority classes does not.

[ช่องของ Toon] This is where your axis “declared vs undeclared” belongs. Evidence for where each paper declares its modification exists for the 7 papers re-read on 16 Oct and in how_obtained_detail of the full re-read.
Evidence: out/data_handling_summary.json (paper-level codes); out/full_summary.json how_obtained_all (entry level, with rules).

The Same Name Is Not the Same Data

Of the 198 dataset names that at least two papers print with a size, 78 appear with more than one size: thyroid with 7,200 instances in five papers and 720 in four, dermatology with 358 (the KEEL version) in eight and 366 (UCI) in two, ecoli with 336, 327, 310 and 301, and pima with 768, 769, 635 and 590. Some of these differences are declared subsamples; the name alone does not tell which. MWMOTE [barua2014mwmote] illustrates the problem inside a single paper: its Satimage (6,435 instances) and Statlandsat (4,435) are the full Statlog Landsat set and its training file, counted as two of its twenty datasets, and its common names are ambiguous in both directions (its Ecoli matches the KEEL file ecoli1 exactly, while its Yeast matches no published split).

Imbalance ratios add a second layer. Table 2 lists the definitions found in the corpus; some are not convertible into one another, and some papers print IR without a formula.

Table 2
Imbalance-Ratio Definitions Printed in the Papers
Definition Formula Used by (examples)
Largest over smallest class \(N_{\max}/N_{\min}\) MDO [abdi2016mdo], CBHSID [palli2022cbhsid], MKC-SMOTE [wang2024mkc] (its \(IR\))
Majority over minority (binary wording) \(N_{\mathrm{maj}}/N_{\mathrm{min}}\) OVO-SMOTE (defined for the binary case, applied to multiclass sets)
Percentage minority \(100\,N_{\min}/N\) RUSBoost [seiffert2010rusboost]
Per-class imbalance degree \(\sum_{q\neq i} N_q/((C-1)N_i)\) OREM-M [zhu2023orem] (overall IR only cited, not printed)
Summed pairwise multiclass IR \(\sum_{i<j} (N_i/N_j - 1)\) SMOM [zhu2017smom], GDHS [yan2025gdhs], MKC-SMOTE (\(IR_{\mathrm{overall}}\))
Imbalance degree \(Id\) distance from uniform [ortigosa-hernandez: not in corpus key to create] SHSampler [zheng2022shsampler] (cited, no formula printed)
Minimum class prior \(N_{\min}/N\) DSRBF [fernandeznavarro2011dsrbf]
Coefficient of variation \(\mathrm{sd}(N_i)/\mathrm{mean}(N_i)\) COG-OS [wu2007cogos]
Proportion pair e.g. \(0.04{:}0.96\) MWMOTE (wording: minority to majority)
Not stated (values equal \(N_{\max}/N_{\min}\)) n/a MC-CCR [koziarski2020mcccr], MC-RBO [krawczyk2020mcrbo]

Errors also travel with shared benchmark tables: MC-CCR and MC-RBO both print an IR of 1.17 for vehicle, a value no definition produces from its class counts.

What the reader should do.

Compare results across papers only after mapping each name to its exact file and class split, and report the IR formula together with its values.

Evidence: out/verified_datasets.csv: names normalised, printed n_instances compared across papers (198 names with a printed size in two or more papers); the earlier 20 of 75 from ai-draft/dataset_variants.json covered 8 papers only and is superseded; mwmote-table5-audit.md; extraction-notes.md; full re-read ir_definition per paper in out/full_summary.json.

Where Reported Wins over SMOTE Come From

Table 3
Per-Dataset Comparisons of the Proposed Method with Plain SMOTE, by How the Dataset Was Obtained. Wins, ties and losses compare printed values under interim rule A (one metric fixed per paper; equal at the printed precision is a tie); scores are not comparable across papers. KNNOR’s single row, a mean over its 19 datasets, is not a per-dataset comparison and is reported in the text instead.
How obtained Rows Papers Proposed wins SMOTE wins Ties
Original 167 26 133 29 5
Repository-defined 119 9 90 13 16
Modified 143 14 109 30 4
Synthetic 5 1 5 0 0
Cannot be told 104 13 82 9 13
Result row not matched to a dataset 3 2 1 1 1
All 541 30 420 82 39

At the paper level, 44 of the 73 papers use plain SMOTE as a baseline, 13 use SMOTE inside a wrapper, and 16 do not compare with SMOTE at all. Fewer papers give rows that can be compared: 30 papers print per-dataset scores for both the proposed method and plain SMOTE in the same table, giving 541 comparisons (Table 3). In these, the proposed method wins in 420 rows, ties in 39 and loses in 82. KNNOR [islam2022knnor] prints only a mean over its 19 datasets (G-score .8363 for KNNOR and .8238 for SMOTE); we report it here as an aggregate result and do not count it as a per-dataset comparison.

Comparisons with SMOTE inside a wrapper are kept apart and are not pooled with Table 3: all 13 wrapper papers print per-dataset pairs, giving 293 rows. In one of them, RBBoost [diezpastor2015randombalance], the extracted pairs do not meet the same-table rule. The scores of its RB-Boost come from the Boosting-family table of its supplement (Supplementary Table 11) and those of its SMOTE ensemble (ESM) from the data-processing-family table (Supplementary Table 3). Both tables report G-mean under one protocol (J48 with Laplace smoothing, ensembles of 100, stratified \(5\times2\)-fold cross-validation), but the paper compares methods only within each family and never compares RB-Boost with ESM directly. Its 86 rows, 63 of them on repository-defined data, are kept in our data for audit and excluded from every comparison set reported here; the other 12 wrapper papers contribute 207 rows.

Split by data type, 29 of the 30 papers include at least one standard dataset (original or repository-defined) in the comparison, and on these 286 standard rows SMOTE wins in 42 and ties in 21. One paper reports its per-dataset comparison with SMOTE only on modified, synthetic or unidentifiable data (INOS [cao2013inos]); KNNOR, whose only comparison is the aggregate above, is not counted here. Conversely, six papers compare only on standard data (GDO [xie2022gdo], MC-MBRC [ma2024mcmbrc], MKC-SMOTE, OREM-M, SCUT [agrawal2015scut], SPE [liu2020spe]).

[ช่องของ Toon] Your hypothesis H1 lives here. Look at the shares of “SMOTE higher” per row of Table 3 and at the per-paper split in the Atlas (fourth tab, wins over SMOTE by data type). What you conclude, and how strongly, is yours; the within-paper comparison (standard vs modified rows of the same paper) is the strongest test because it holds the paper constant.

A method that wins on unmodified standard benchmarks gives the reader evidence that does not depend on choices the authors made about the data. Reporting the standard and the modified datasets separately would let readers see this directly.

Evidence: out/verified_outcomes.csv (smote_kind = plain SMOTE; KNNOR’s aggregate, row 295, set aside by rule R4); counts reproduced by build/reconcile_counts.py (out/reconcile_counts.json). Of the 541 rows, 3 could not be matched to a dataset entry and 15 were matched by row order only (over all 835 rows: 4 and 22). Paper-level baselines: out/full_summary.json, papers, smote_kind. RBBoost: rows 574–659; supplement Table 3 pp.3–5 and Table 11 pp.17–18; protocol p.101 and family design p.102 of the paper; review recorded in CROSS_TABLE_REVIEW of build/reconcile_counts.py.

Of the 57 papers that use SMOTE as a baseline (44 plain, 13 wrapped), 13 give a reader no per-dataset pair of scores in the paper itself: the results are plots (Borderline-SMOTE [han2005borderline], Safe-Level-SMOTE [bunkhumpornpat2009safelevel], Cluster-SMOTE [cieslak2006cluster], k-means SMOTE [douzas2018kmeans], GLOS [han2023glos]), averages (G-SMOTE [douzas2019gsmote], CISO [yadav2025ciso], SplitBal [sun2015splitbal], QC-SMOTE [upman2026qcsmote]), or ranks (MDO, RBO [koziarski2019rbo], MC-NCLWO [tao2025mcnclwo]), and the review by Hassanat et al. [hassanat2022stop] compares synthetic points rather than classifiers. A fourteenth paper, KNNOR, prints its pair of scores only as a mean over its datasets.

QC-SMOTE copies its baseline numbers from the VS-SMOTE paper [vs-smote: not in corpus key to create], and every SMOTE-all value in MC-CCR’s Table 6 is identical, to two decimals and on all 20 datasets, to the SMOTE-all column of MC-RBO’s Table VI, from the same group and with the same C5.0 setup. Several of these papers place per-dataset results on GitHub or in material outside the paper.   1. Name the repository and version of every dataset, and whether the full set or a training file was used.

  2. State which class or classes form the minority and why, in the text and not only in a table.

  3. Declare every modification (binarisation, class merging, undersampling, noise, dropped attributes) in the data section.

  4. Give the imbalance-ratio formula, not only its values.

  5. Report per-dataset results for the proposed method and plain SMOTE, and report standard and modified datasets separately.

  6. Separate tuning datasets from evaluation datasets, as CISO and LS [cieslak2008ls] do, and run the baselines rather than copying their numbers.

\section{How the SMOTE Literature Uses Data}
\label{sec:data}

A reader who wants to compare two SMOTE variants, or to choose a benchmark for a
new one, needs answers to questions that the papers rarely answer together.
Can the numbers that two papers report on a dataset of the same name be
compared? How broad is the evidence behind the benchmarks the field relies on?
When a paper reports that its method beats SMOTE, on what kind of data does
that happen, and can a reader check it? This section answers these questions
from the 1,654 dataset entries and 835 comparisons with SMOTE
(834 per dataset and one average over datasets) that we extracted from the 76 papers of
our corpus. Three of them (ENN, AdaBoost and one review) contain no
evaluation on data, so counts below use the 73 papers with an
evaluation on data; Tomek links is kept because it illustrates its method on
one synthetic two-class set.

\claudedraft{The central observation is that the evidence for a new oversampler
is only as interpretable as the description of its data, and in this
literature that description is often incomplete: the same name can denote
different tasks, modifications are frequently undeclared, and a sizeable share
of papers report results that cannot be traced back to individual datasets.}

% ---------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Extraction Procedure}
\label{sec:data-method}
For every paper we read the full text and any supplementary file in our
collection, and recorded each dataset as printed, including spelling, with
its group in the paper, source repository, size, number of features and
classes, minority and majority counts, and the imbalance ratio where the
paper prints them, together with the table and page they come from. For each
dataset we also recorded how it reached the experiment:
\emph{original} (used as distributed, with its native classes),
\emph{repository-defined} (a two-class split published by a repository such
as KEEL or imbalanced-learn, used as is), \emph{modified} (the authors chose
the minority classes, merged or dropped classes, set a threshold, undersampled
or injected noise), or \emph{synthetic} (generated by the authors). Where a
paper did not state its source, two fixed rules were applied and flagged:
names that follow the KEEL file convention (for example
\texttt{ecoli-0-1\_vs\_5}, \texttt{yeast4}) were labelled repository-defined,
and common names in multiclass papers with no stated change were labelled
original. Two further rules were fixed before counting: a set that is two-class
in its source and is used without comment was labelled original, and a set from
which the authors removed rows (for example, records with missing values) or
attributes was labelled modified.

For the results we copied, per dataset, the printed score of the proposed
method and of SMOTE from one results table selected by a fixed rule:
G-mean, else AUC, else F-measure, else accuracy; the classifier highlighted
in the abstract, else the first reported; the unperturbed condition. We
recorded values rather than wins so that any definition of a win can be
applied later. Plain SMOTE was distinguished from SMOTE embedded in a
multiclass or ensemble wrapper (Static-SMOTE, OVO-SMOTE~\pcite{fernandez2013analysing}, SMOTE-all,
SMOTE+AdaBoost). Values printed in a paper are never overwritten; corrections
against the source repository are stored beside them with their justification.
Every extracted value was then checked against the PDF a second time: a value
was accepted when the dataset name and its numbers appear on the same line of
the cited page, and every table that is printed as an image or whose text layer
is garbled was read from the rendered page instead. All 1,654 dataset entries
and 835 comparisons passed this check.

out/full\_uncertain.csv, each resolved in out/uncertain\_resolution.csv; second check:
build/verify\_pdf.py, out/visual\_checks.json, out/verified\_*.csv.}
